DALLAS COUNTY CLERK'S OFFICE
─────────────────────
Original business registration, March 3rd, 1902.

Entity registered as THORESON & HARTLEY TOYS — equal partnership between William A. Thoreson and Robert J. Hartley. No dissolution paperwork ever filed. No record of any buyout or transfer.

— J. Fowler, Dallas County Clerk

DALLAS COUNTY CORONER'S OFFICE
─────────────────────
Preliminary autopsy on Thoreson complete. Toxicology out until Thursday.

Full report faxed to the residence. Someone with medical training should interpret it.

Also — small brass key found in the deceased's left jacket pocket. Sending it back with you.

— F. Garrett, Dallas County Coroner

PINKERTON NATIONAL DETECTIVE AGENCY
─────────────────────
Background checks complete. Two items of note.

SUBJECT 1: {{walter_lippman}} — pen name only. Legal name Taylor James Hartley, born March 5th 1911, Dallas TX.

SUBJECT 2: {{miranda_longfellow}} — legal name change filed 1920. Born Miranda Elaine Hartley, 1896, Dallas TX.

— Pinkerton National Detective Agency, Dallas Office

You have always believed the truth is better than comfortable silence.

knowledge.text: You recognize what killed William Thoreson. Check your Expert Notes — you know exactly what this means and where it comes from.

memories.text: You were there in 1902 when William Thoreson and Robert Hartley announced their partnership. You remember shaking Robert's hand. A serious man. You never saw Robert again after 1910, and nobody in this city had the decency to ask why.

You remember the original incorporation — Thoreson and Hartley, equal shares. Within a year the Hartley name had quietly disappeared. William said the partnership dissolved by mutual agreement. You did not believe that then.

canShare.text: In my circles, there were always whispers about a woman named Margaret connected to the Thoresons. Nobody ever knew the details.

Accounting.title: Financial Ledger Analysis
Accounting.errorMsg: Incorrect password. Find someone with the proper expertise.
Accounting.summary: The ledger contains secret monthly payments of $50 to someone listed only as 'T.H.' — going back to 1911. The payments were authorized personally by Will, bypassing normal accounting. Over 24 years of hidden disbursements to an unknown recipient.
Accounting.expert:
I've conducted a thorough review of the 1934 financial ledger for Thoreson Toys. On the surface, the books appear orderly — routine vendor payments, service fees, equipment maintenance, and quarterly sales revenue deposits. The company appears profitable, with a healthy year-end balance.

However, buried among the legitimate entries is a recurring anomaly that would be invisible to an untrained eye:

On the 5th of every month, there is a payment of exactly $50.00 listed as "Monthly Disbursement — T.H." This payment has no corresponding invoice, no vendor record, and no business justification anywhere in these books. It appears in every single month without exception.

This is deeply irregular. In proper bookkeeping, every disbursement must be tied to a payee, a purchase order, or an account. Using only initials — "T.H." — is a deliberate attempt to obscure the identity of the recipient. Furthermore, these payments are authorized personally by W. Thoreson himself, bypassing the normal approval chain entirely.

Cross-referencing with the ledger's date entries, these payments appear to have been ongoing since at least 1911 — over twenty-four years of secret monthly payments to someone William Thoreson did not want anyone to know about.

This is not a business expense. Fifty dollars a month, paid without fail for over two decades, personally authorized and deliberately hidden — this is a private obligation. Whoever "T.H." is, William Thoreson has been supporting them in secret for a very long time.

Recommendation: Determine the identity of "T.H." — the initials may refer to a person, possibly someone connected to the Thoreson family. The consistency and secrecy of these payments suggest a deeply personal matter — a debt, an obligation, or someone he felt responsible for.

French.title: Margaret's Letter (Translated)
French.lockedSubtitle: This letter is written entirely in French
French.errorMsg: Incorrect password. Find someone who speaks French.
French.header: Letter from Margaret Hartley to William Thoreson
French.summary: A letter from Margaret Hartley to Will, written in French. She confronts him over the secrets he kept and the people he abandoned. She mentions a safe in the study with a combination that meant something to him.
French.expert:
This letter was written in French — likely deliberately, so that only someone educated abroad would be able to read it. The tone is deeply personal, angry, and accusatory. Here is the full translation:

"June 4th, 1914

William,

You always kept your secrets locked away. Just like that safe in your hallway closet. I know you have a heart in there somewhere. Even though you showed no heart when you sent me away.

I wonder — does the combination reveal how you truly felt? Our son turned three this past March and you were not there. You locked his birthday behind steel and numbers because you could not bring yourself to forget it, and you could not bring yourself to claim it.

Our son deserved a father. You gave him money and a name on a trust document and nothing else. He will grow up not knowing who he is because you decided your reputation mattered more than his life.

I have given everything to keep him safe. You have given nothing but silence and a monthly check.

I have kept your secret all these years. But secrets have a way of rising to the surface, William. Especially yours.

— Margaret"

Margaret is furious — and grief-stricken. She confronts Will directly over their child — a son he funded privately but refused to acknowledge. Will chose secrecy over fatherhood.

Margaret references a safe in the hallway closet. The letter is dated June 1914. She says their son turned three this past March. Three years old in March 1914 means the child was born in March 1911. The combination is his birthday — we just need the exact day.

Legal.title: Forged Transfer Documents
Legal.lockedSubtitle: This document requires legal expertise to examine
Legal.errorMsg: Incorrect password. Find someone with legal knowledge.
Legal.summary: The company ownership transfer from Robert Hartley to Will Thoreson is fraudulent. Robert's signature doesn't match known samples, the document is dated one day before Robert's death, and the notary 'James Crawford' has no record in Dallas County.
Legal.expert:
I've examined this ownership transfer document purporting to convey Robert Hartley's fifty-percent stake in the company to William Thoreson. At first glance it appears to be a standard business transfer, but upon closer inspection, there are multiple red flags that call its legitimacy into serious question.

The signature attributed to Robert Hartley is forged. The pen strokes are hesitant and show signs of tracing — inconsistent with someone's natural handwriting. The ink also appears slightly different in color and weight from the body of the document, suggesting it was added at a different time, possibly after the document was drafted.

The timing is deeply suspicious. The document is dated March 13, 1910 — two days before Robert Hartley's death. A man transferring his entire stake in a profitable company two days before he dies, with no apparent consideration or payment recorded? That defies all standard business practice.

I also attempted to verify the witness. The document bears the signature of "James Crawford, Notary Public." However, there is no record of any James Crawford serving as a licensed notary in Dallas County during this period. The notary seal, upon close examination, appears hand-stamped rather than embossed — another indication of fabrication.

In my professional opinion, this document is fraudulent. Robert Hartley did not willingly sign over his company. Someone — almost certainly William Thoreson — forged this transfer to seize full ownership of what was originally a shared business. This was theft.

Medical.title: Autopsy — Cause of Death
Medical.lockedSubtitle: This document requires medical expertise to interpret
Medical.errorMsg: Incorrect password. Find someone with medical knowledge.
Medical.header: Preliminary Autopsy Report — William Thoreson Sr.
Medical.summary: Will died of acute Aconitine poisoning — a toxin from Wolfsbane. It was administered orally, likely in food or drink. Symptoms include numbness, weakness, and cardiac arrest within 2-6 hours. This was murder.
Medical.expert:
I've reviewed the preliminary autopsy findings in detail. The external examination showed no signs of trauma, struggle, or forced ingestion — which initially supported the assumption of natural causes. However, the toxicology results tell a very different story.

Cause of Death: Acute poisoning. Toxicology indicates the presence of Aconitine — a lethal alkaloid derived from the plant Aconitum, commonly known as Wolfsbane or Monkshood. Concentration levels in the blood are consistent with a single, deliberate oral dose.

Aconitine is extraordinarily dangerous — among the most potent plant-based poisons known to medicine. It disrupts sodium channels in nerve and heart tissue, causing progressive paralysis of the cardiac muscle. Based on the concentration found, the victim would have experienced initial tingling or numbness in the mouth and throat within minutes of ingestion, followed by increasing weakness, nausea, and a sense of dread. Within two to six hours, complete cardiac arrest.

This was not natural causes. This was not an accident. The dose was precise and deliberate — someone with knowledge of the poison administered it orally, almost certainly dissolved into food or drink. William Thoreson was murdered.

One additional note of medical significance: Aconitine leaves very little trace and is easily missed in a standard examination. Had this autopsy not included a full toxicology panel, the death would likely have been ruled cardiac failure. Whoever chose this poison knew exactly what they were doing.

Note: Aconitine is derived from Wolfsbane, a plant that grows wild in the mountainous regions of Europe — particularly the Alps of Switzerland, Austria, and Northern Italy.

Banking.title: Bank Statement Analysis — Kessler & Braun Investment
Banking.lockedSubtitle: These financial records require banking expertise to interpret
Banking.errorMsg: Incorrect password. Find someone with banking experience.
Banking.summary: An $8,000 wire transfer was sent to Kessler & Braun European Distributors in Hamburg for an overseas expansion deal. The company dissolved within six weeks — total loss. Two outside investors had money in Thoreson Toys when it happened.
Banking.expert:
I've been looking over the Thoreson Toys bank statements. Most of this is what you'd expect — weekly sales deposits, payroll, vendor payments. The company's been running steady for years. But a few things caught my eye.

First — right at the top of the statement, January 2nd. Two outside investors deposited money into the company account. Investor Account 7714-A put in $3,000 and Investor Account 7722-B put in $2,500. That's $5,500 of other people's money that Will was managing.

Then in March, there's a wire transfer for $8,000 sent to a company called Kessler & Braun European Distributors out of Hamburg, Germany. Looks like Will was trying to break into overseas markets — European toy distribution. That's a big swing for a company this size. The account dropped from $22,000 down to about $14,000 overnight.

Six weeks later, Kessler & Braun's account was dissolved. There's a write-down on the books for the full $8,000 — total loss. No recovered funds, nothing coming back. Just gone.

Now here's where it gets interesting. After the loss hit the books, both of those investor accounts went quiet. No additional deposits. No withdrawals. Just silence. Somebody lost real money because of Will's decision, and Will never made it right. He just kept running the company as if nothing happened.

The question is — who are these two investors, and are they here tonight?

Botany.title: Botanical Analysis — Wolfsbane
Botany.lockedSubtitle: This requires botanical expertise to identify
Botany.summary: The poison is Aconitine, derived from Wolfsbane — Aconitum napellus. This plant does not grow in Texas or anywhere in North America. It is native to the Alpine regions of Europe. Whoever used this poison traveled to obtain it deliberately.
Botany.expert:
Genus: Aconitum — Family Ranunculaceae. Common names: Wolfsbane, Monkshood, Devil's Helmet. Every part of this plant is lethally toxic. The roots contain the highest concentration of aconitine, but the flowers, leaves, and stems are equally dangerous if handled carelessly or ingested.

I have known this plant since childhood. My grandmother kept a botanical encyclopedia and made me memorize the most dangerous specimens before I was allowed in the garden unsupervised. Aconitum was at the top of the list — she called it the queen of poisons, a name it has carried since antiquity. The ancient Romans used it for executions. Medieval assassins favored it. It has been killing people, accidentally and deliberately, for two thousand years.

The active compound, aconitine, works by binding irreversibly to sodium channels in nerve and cardiac tissue. It does not announce itself. The initial symptoms — numbness at the lips and tongue, a metallic taste, mild warmth — are easily mistaken for indigestion or anxiety. Within thirty minutes to an hour, the numbness spreads. The victim's hands and face begin to feel detached. Breathing becomes labored. The heart, which relies on those same sodium channels to regulate its rhythm, begins to fail. Death typically follows within two to six hours of ingestion, and it looks, to the untrained eye, like a heart attack.

This is not a plant you stumble upon in a Dallas garden. Aconitum does not grow in Texas. It does not grow anywhere in North America. It is native to mountain meadows at high elevation — the Swiss Alps, the Austrian highlands, the Pyrenees. The flowers are distinctive: deep violet-blue, hooded, unmistakably beautiful. A person would have to travel to those regions, recognize the plant, harvest it deliberately, and transport the extract home. This was not opportunistic. This required planning months in advance.

The method of administration almost certainly involved the extract dissolved into food or drink — something with a strong enough flavor to mask the initial bitterness. A cocktail. A rich sauce. Something with sweetness or acid. The victim would have noticed nothing unusual until the symptoms were already well underway.

One final note: aconitine is notoriously difficult to detect in a standard post-mortem examination. Without a toxicologist specifically looking for alkaloid poisoning, this death would have been recorded as cardiac failure. Whoever chose this poison knew that. This was chosen by someone with patience, knowledge, and access to Alpine Europe.

Journalism.title: Newspaper Article — Hartley Death
Journalism.lockedSubtitle: A trained journalist might notice things others would miss
Journalism.errorMsg: Incorrect password. Find someone with journalism experience.
Journalism.summary: This article has problems. The investigation was closed in under 24 hours despite a suspicious business transfer the day before. The sourcing is thin and Thoreson's quote sounds rehearsed. Someone with influence shaped this story.
Journalism.expert:
I've read a lot of newspaper copy in my career. This article is wrong in ways that only a journalist would notice.

First — the timeline. Robert Hartley was found dead on March 15th, 1910. The investigation was opened and closed by March 22nd. That's seven days to investigate the death of a prominent businessman with an active partnership dispute. No coroner's inquest mentioned. No witness testimony cited. No follow-up promised. That is not thorough reporting — that is a story someone wanted finished.

Second — the sourcing. The only named source in this article is William Thoreson himself. His quote reads like it was prepared in advance: measured, sympathetic, careful. There's no quote from the police investigator, no comment from Hartley's family, no statement from anyone at the company. A real reporter would have talked to at least three people. This reporter talked to one — the man who stood to benefit most from Hartley's death.

Third — and this is the part that should trouble everyone in this room — the article makes no mention of the ownership transfer document filed two days before Robert died. March 13th: Robert's entire stake in the company is signed over to Thoreson. March 15th: Robert is dead. Any competent journalist would have connected those two facts. This one didn't. Either they weren't told, or they were told not to ask.

Finally — the framing. The headline says "Thoreson Cleared." Not "Hartley Death Ruled Suicide." Not "Investigation Closed." The story is framed around Thoreson's innocence, not around what happened to Robert Hartley. That tells you who this article was written for.

Someone with influence shaped this coverage. The question is whether it was Thoreson himself or someone acting on his behalf.

items.title: Bradford Patent Letter
items.summary: A letter dated January 1935 from Bradford & Sons Toy Company. Thomas Bradford claims a spring-loaded mechanism in Thoreson Toys' newest line was patented by his company in 1931 and demands compensation. Will's handwritten margin note reads: 'Frivolous. Have Scott handle.'

items.title: Original Incorporation Filing
items.summary: Dallas County filing dated April 3, 1902. Lists William Thoreson and Robert Hartley as equal 50/50 partners under the name Thoreson & Hartley Toys. Both signatures present and notarized.

items.title: Company Transfer Document
items.summary: A transfer document dated March 13, 1910 signing Robert Hartley's full ownership over to William Thoreson. Notarized by one James Crawford. Requires a Legal expert to examine.

items.title: Bank Statement — Thoreson Toys Capital Account
items.summary: A 1934 bank statement for the Thoreson Toys company account. Shows two investor deposits totaling $5,500 in January, followed by an $8,000 wire transfer to Kessler & Braun European Distributors in Hamburg in March. The account dropped from $22,000 to $14,000 overnight. Requires Banking expertise to fully analyze.

items.title: The Stolen Company
items.summary: The transfer document has been examined. The signature is forged — Robert Hartley never signed it. The notary James Crawford does not appear in Dallas County records.

items.title: Financial Ledger
items.summary: Company financial ledger going back to 1911. Contains a recurring monthly entry of $50 listed as 'Monthly Disbursement — T.H.' — appearing every month for over 24 years. Requires an Accounting expert to examine.

items.title: Margaret's Letter
items.summary: A letter written entirely in French, addressed to William Thoreson and signed by Margaret. Requires a French speaker to translate.

items.title: Birth Certificate — Taylor Hartley
items.summary: Dallas County birth certificate. Name: Taylor Hartley. Date of birth: March 5, 1911. Mother: Margaret Hartley. Father: William S. Thoreson. Registered March 11, 1911. County Clerk: Edgar T. Calloway.

items.title: Newspaper — Margaret Hartley Obituary
items.summary: A brief obituary from a Dallas newspaper, dated October 14, 1914. Margaret Hartley, formerly of Dallas, passed away leaving behind two children. Cause of death listed as accidental overdose of laudanum. No mention of surviving family beyond the children.

items.title: Will Thoreson's Last Will & Testament
items.summary: A will dated January 14, 1935, dividing the estate equally into three shares — one each to William Scott Thoreson Jr., Frederick Daniel Thoreson, and Taylor Hartley. Taylor Hartley is described as a recognized heir whose claim upon the estate Will acknowledges 'fully and without reservation.'

items.title: The Secret Heir
items.summary: The ledger entries, bank statement, and birth certificate have been cross-referenced. 'T.H.' refers to Taylor Hartley — a child born to Margaret Hartley in 1911, with the father listed as unknown. Will has been making private payments to an account in Taylor Hartley's name since that year.

items.title: Coroner's Report
items.summary: Preliminary autopsy report on William Thoreson. Notes unusual cardiac presentation. Requires a Medical expert to interpret.

items.title: The Poison Identified
items.summary: Aconitine was found in the body of William Thoreson — confirmed by the coroner's report. Our botanist has determined that Aconitine is derived from Wolfsbane, a rare flower that grows exclusively in the Swiss Alps. It cannot be purchased or sourced in North America. Someone had to travel there to obtain it.

items.title: Miranda's Travel Journal
items.summary: A personal journal belonging to Miranda Longfellow, covering her trip to Switzerland in summer 1934. One entry dated August 14 reads: 'The flowers in the Alps are remarkable — one of which definitely caught my eye.'

items.title: Pinkerton Background Check Results
items.summary: Pinkerton report on all party guests. Two name changes flagged: Walter Lippman — legal name Taylor James Hartley, born 1911, name changed 1930. Miranda Longfellow — legal name Miranda Elaine Hartley, born 1896, name changed 1920.

items.title: Miranda Unmasked
items.summary: Miranda Longfellow's legal name is Miranda Hartley. She is the daughter of Robert Hartley — Will's former business partner. She changed her name in 1920 and has worked as Scott's legal assistant for the past ten years.

priority1.base:
You are the killer.

Your connection to the Hartley family runs deeper than anyone in this room knows. Robert Hartley's story — the stolen company, the forged documents, the death that was ruled a suicide — is not abstract history to you. It is personal. You have spent years getting close enough to confirm what you always suspected, and planning what you would do when the moment came.

Last summer you traveled to Switzerland. Wolfsbane grows wild in the Alps — purple flowers along the mountain trails, beautiful and poisonous down to the root. You brought some home. You dried it. You ground it.

Tonight, before the guests arrived, you put it in his drink.

William is dead. You are at peace with that. You are not a villain. You are someone who was owed a debt that was never going to be paid any other way.

You are good at stillness. Let the investigation find you. Help where you can. The slower the truth comes out, the better the story.

access.miranda_longfellow: Ten years as legal manager of the Thoreson estate gave you access to every document William thought was safely hidden. You read everything. You filed everything. You knew exactly where the forged transfer was kept, where the ledger lived, where the love letters were locked. Your access was total and completely unremarkable — you were just the help.
access.walter_lippman: You spent years covering Dallas business, circling the Thoreson story from the outside, never able to confirm what you suspected. Then William invited you personally. You came because you thought you were finally going to get the story. Instead you decided to end it. You had already obtained the wolfsbane before the invitation arrived. The invitation just gave you the room.
access.vivienne_ashford: You grew up in and out of this house. You know which doors lock, which drawers stick, where things are kept. Coming back from abroad gave you distance — and distance gave you clarity about what this family had done and who had paid for it. You had time in Europe to confirm what you suspected and to find what you needed in the Swiss Alps. Coming home was always going to end like this.
access.raymond_hammond: Fifteen years as business manager gave you access to every part of this company except the books. But you knew the building. You knew the schedules. You knew when William was alone and when he wasn't. You knew which drinks William preferred and who prepared them. Proximity is its own kind of access — and you had been proximate for fifteen years.
access.elizabeth_monroe: You have been inside Dallas society for forty years. You knew the Hartley family before the scandal. You were there when Robert died. You watched William walk away clean and build an empire on what he took. You have been patient for a very long time. Nobody watches the most fun person in the room.
access.marcus_brennan: You did not invest in Thoreson Toys for the returns. You invested to get close. Four years inside the company gave you everything you needed — access to William, to the building, to the drinks service at company events. The European deal collapsing was an inconvenience. What you came here to do tonight was always the plan.

priority2.base:
You are the secret heir.

You may not know this yet — or you have suspected it without being able to confirm it. There was always something unexplained. A trust fund with no clear origin. A family connection that was never fully spelled out. A feeling that the story of where you came from had a chapter nobody would show you.

William Thoreson invited you tonight specifically. He said he had an announcement — something that concerned you personally. You came because some part of you has always known this night was coming.

You are connected to William Thoreson in a way that is about to become very public. Let the investigation find this. Do not lead it there. Your reaction when it surfaces should feel genuine — because in many ways, it is.

access.miranda_longfellow: You grew up knowing you were Robert Hartley's daughter. What you discovered after years working inside the Thoreson files was that Margaret's second child — the one William funded secretly — was your half-sibling. The heir story is more complicated for you than for anyone else in this room.
access.walter_lippman: You were born Taylor Hartley on March 5th, 1911. Your mother was Margaret. You were raised by distant relatives after Margaret died, told very little about where you came from, only that there was a trust fund in your name. You built a career. You never stopped looking for the story. Tonight you are going to find it.
access.vivienne_ashford: The Ashford family connection to the Thoresons goes back further than anyone has said. You were raised knowing less than you should about your own family history. Coming back from abroad, you started asking questions that nobody wanted to answer. Tonight some of them will be answered whether anyone wants them to be or not.
access.raymond_hammond: You grew up with a trust fund that nobody could fully explain. You changed your name when you were young — the name you were born with carried something uncomfortable that nobody would talk about. You applied for the business manager position at Thoreson Toys without knowing the connection. You have been inside this company for fifteen years without understanding why it always felt personal.
access.elizabeth_monroe: You have spent forty years in Dallas society carefully curating who you are and where you came from. The truth is considerably more complicated. Your family's connection to the Hartleys predates the scandal — and what William did in 1910 had consequences for your family that you have never spoken about publicly.
access.marcus_brennan: You know exactly who you are and what you are doing here. When you discovered the truth about your origins — the Hartley connection, the trust fund, what William had done — you made a plan. You invested the trust money back into Thoreson Toys deliberately. Four years inside the company. Four years watching. Tonight William was going to make his announcement. You wanted to be in the room when it happened.

facts.text: William Thoreson founded Thoreson Toys in 1902. It is now one of the largest toy companies in Texas, employing over two hundred people across three facilities.
Thoreson Toys is known for quality wooden toys and games. William built the company's reputation personally — he knew every buyer, every supplier, and every employee by name.

Six months ago, a major European distribution deal collapsed. The company took a significant financial loss. William became quieter and more private afterward. Two investors began sending demand letters.
William always kept the company's financial ledgers personally. Even the business manager never had full access to the books. Nobody ever thought much of it until now.
William Thoreson was a commanding presence — generous in public, demanding in private. He expected excellence from everyone around him, including his children. He was not a man who apologized easily.
William told several people that tonight was going to be a special evening — that he had an important announcement to make. He said he was finally going to make something right. He did not say what.
{{scott_thoreson}} has been managing the day-to-day operations of Thoreson Toys for the past two years. William was stepping back — some said by choice, others said by necessity.

The Thoresons are one of Dallas's most prominent families. William has been a fixture of the city's business and charity circles for thirty years. An invitation to the estate is considered a mark of distinction.
{{dorothy_wells}} has lived in Dallas longer than almost anyone here. If something happened in this city in the last fifty years, there is a reasonable chance {{dorothy_wells}} was in the room.
{{miranda_longfellow}} has managed the legal affairs of the Thoreson estate for nearly ten years. Every significant document, contract, and filing has passed through those hands.

{{david_richardson}} is a licensed private investigator and a Thoreson cousin. The moment something goes wrong at a family gathering, {{david_richardson}} starts making calls. It is a reflex at this point.
William always drank the same thing at his own gatherings — a specific bourbon, neat, prepared by the household before guests arrived. He rarely varied from it.
William had been in good health for a man his age. No serious illness, no medications that anyone knew of. His death tonight is not a natural event.

cocktail.text: Find {{david_richardson}} before the evening begins. Rumor has it there is a private investigator at the party tonight. Find out why.
cocktail.complete: You introduced yourself to {{david_richardson}}. Something about the way {{david_richardson}} looked at you suggested this would not be your last conversation tonight.

cocktail.text: Introduce yourself to {{walter_lippman}} and find out what story brought a journalist to a private dinner party. William did not invite people without reason.
cocktail.complete: {{walter_lippman}} was cagey about the invitation. Said William had reached out personally. That is worth remembering.

cocktail.text: Find {{miranda_longfellow}} — the person who manages all the Thoreson legal affairs. Ask what William has been working on lately. Legal managers always know more than they say.
cocktail.complete: {{miranda_longfellow}} said everything was routine. Said it with a perfectly straight face. You are not sure you believed it.

cocktail.text: Seek out {{charles_sterling}}. An old friend of William's with decades in Dallas banking. Ask what he knows about the company's recent financial troubles.
cocktail.complete: {{charles_sterling}} chose words carefully. Said the European situation was complicated. Said William had been under unusual pressure. Did not say more.

cocktail.text: Find {{vivienne_ashford}} — just returned from years abroad. Ask what brought someone home after so long. People who leave and come back always have a reason.
cocktail.complete: {{vivienne_ashford}} said something about family obligation. Then changed the subject. The way {{vivienne_ashford}} looked at the house suggested more than that.

cocktail.text: Find {{marcus_brennan}} and ask about the investment in Thoreson Toys. The European deal collapse cost people real money. Find out how angry they actually are.
cocktail.complete: {{marcus_brennan}} said losing money was one thing. Said being lied to was another. Said tonight was supposed to be about answers.

cocktail.text: Introduce yourself to {{dorothy_wells}}. The most senior person in the room, with the longest memory in Dallas. Ask what {{dorothy_wells}} remembers about the early days of Thoreson Toys.
cocktail.complete: {{dorothy_wells}} smiled and said the early days were interesting ones. Said there had been another name involved, once. Did not say which.

cocktail.text: Find {{victoria_ashworth}} and take the measure of the room's most analytical mind. Ask what {{victoria_ashworth}} makes of tonight's gathering. Investors notice things other people miss.
cocktail.complete: {{victoria_ashworth}} said William had been evasive for months. Said that was unusual for a man who prided himself on directness. Said something felt off about tonight before anything happened.

cocktail.text: Introduce yourself to three people you have not spoken to yet — in character. You are not yourself tonight. Tell them who you are, how you know William, and why you are here.
cocktail.complete: Three conversations. Three new faces. The evening is beginning to take shape.

cocktail.text: Ask two different guests what they think of William Thoreson. Not the official version — the honest one. People tell you things at parties they would not say anywhere else.
cocktail.complete: Two perspectives. Neither of them simple. William Thoreson was clearly not a simple man.

cocktail.text: William told several people he had an important announcement tonight. Find someone who knows what it was. Start asking questions — carefully.
cocktail.complete: Nobody seems to know exactly what the announcement was. But everyone seems to have a theory.

cocktail.text: The European distribution deal collapse has been the talk of Dallas business circles for months. Find out who in this room was affected — and how angry they still are.
cocktail.complete: More people than you expected had skin in that deal. The money was one thing. The silence from William afterward was another.

cocktail.text: By the end of cocktail hour, find out one thing about another guest that they probably did not intend to reveal. Every party has loose lips if you know how to listen.
cocktail.complete: You found something. File it away. Tonight is young.

cocktail.text: Identify one person in this room you think you can trust. You may need allies before the night is over. Choose carefully.
cocktail.complete: You have a candidate. Whether that trust is earned remains to be seen.

cocktail.text: By the end of cocktail hour, identify one person in this room who makes you uneasy. You cannot explain it yet. Trust the instinct.
cocktail.complete: You have someone in mind. Whether you are right is a different question entirely.

cocktail.text: Try to establish where William was in the last hour before dinner was to be served. Who spoke to him? Who saw him? When was he last seen alive?
cocktail.complete: A picture is beginning to form. Imperfect. But a beginning.

CIN_SECTIONS.text: "As many of you know, my father invited you here for a dinner party. He said he had an announcement to make — something that would change everything."

"Most of you know my father. William Thoreson. He built this family from nothing — came to Dallas in 1899 with very little and spent the next thirty years turning it into something. Thoreson Toys. Started in a workshop on Commerce Street in 1902. By 1920, one of the most successful toy manufacturers in the Southwest. By 1930, his name was on buildings."
"He was a self-made man. That is how he told it. That is how everyone told it."
"He was found earlier this evening. I do not know how. I do not know why. The authorities have been contacted, but due to the storm, we are on our own for now."
"No one leaves until we understand what happened."
"I am Scott Thoreson — his eldest son. I have handled this family's legal affairs for years. I never imagined I would be investigating my own father's death. But here we are. And I need your help."

"Some of you have particular expertise. If you find something you cannot make sense of, look for someone who can. Some documents require specific skills to interpret. If you find a QR code, scan it in the app — but you will need the right skill to unlock it."
"The goal is simple: find out what happened to my father. His business, his dealings, anything that might explain why someone in this room wanted him dead."
"The Living Room, Dining Room, Parlor, Kitchen, Breakfast Nook, and my father's Office are all open."

presentation.openingHtml:
Dallas, Texas · 1935
Case No. ——
Thor's Murder Mysteries
A DEATH AT THE ESTATE
William Thoreson Sr. is dead. The investigation begins.
Address by
Scott Thoreson Jr.
● Live
The Announcement

Stand where everyone can see you. Take a breath.

"Thank you all for coming tonight."

Look around the room.

"As many of you know, my father invited you here for a dinner party. He said he had an announcement to make — something that would "change everything.""

"Most of you know my father. William Thoreson. He built this family from nothing — came to Dallas in 1899 with very little and spent the next thirty years turning it into something."

"Thoreson Toys. Started in a workshop on Commerce Street in 1902. By 1920 it was one of the most successful toy manufacturers in the Southwest. By 1930, his name was on buildings."

"He was a self-made man. That's how he told it. That's how everyone told it."

Longer pause. Let confusion set in.

"My father... William Thoreson... is dead."

Let that land. Wait for reactions.

"He was found earlier this evening. I don't know how. I don't know why. The authorities have been contacted, but due to the storm, we're on our own for now."

"No one leaves until we understand what happened."

"I'm Scott Thoreson — his eldest son. I've handled this family's legal affairs for years. I never imagined I'd be investigating my own father's death."

"But here we are. And I need your help."

The Rules

More businesslike now — still in character, but organizing.

"Here's how this will work."

"We'll investigate in phases. After each phase, I'll call everyone back together to share what we've found."

"Some rooms are open now. Others are closed — if a door is closed, it's off limits for now."

"You'll see blue tape on certain items. Those are personal belongings. Please respect them."

"Some of you may have particular expertise. If you find something you can't make sense of, look for someone who can. Some documents require specific knowledge to interpret."

"If you find a document with a QR code, scan it with your app — but you'll need the right skill. Find the person with the right expertise."

"If you want to search another guest — and you might — come to me first. We'll handle it properly."

"The goal is simple: find out what happened to my father."

"Let's start by learning what we can about him. His business. His dealings. Anything that might explain why someone would want him dead."

Final look around.

"The Living Room, Dining Room, Parlor, Kitchen, Breakfast Nook, and my father's Office are all open."

"Begin."

Investigation

pages.netsuke:
Side Quest
The Netsuke Case
A Matter of Personal Honor

Rupert Thoreson — Will's twin brother and the estate's unofficial photographer — is the proud owner of a remarkable collection of Japanese Netsuke: hand-carved ivory and boxwood toggles from the Edo period. Frogs. Dragons. Merchants. Monks. Each one small enough to fit in a closed fist. Each one irreplaceable.

Somewhere on the premises this evening, a small brass key has gone missing. It could be anywhere. A coat pocket. A side table. Wedged between sofa cushions. Sitting on a windowsill where someone set it down without thinking.

Find the key. Return it to Rupert. Try not to make a big deal of it — he'll be embarrassed enough as it is.
